title: The Goal Is Love, and Mercy to the Worst of Sinners
summary: Paul reminds Timothy why he left him in Ephesus: to stop certain men from teaching false doctrines built on myths, genealogies, and a misuse of the law. He explains that the law is good when used rightly, then gives thanks for the mercy that turned him, a former persecutor, into an apostle, since Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. The chapter closes with a charge to Timothy to fight the good fight and a warning drawn from two men who have shipwrecked their faith.
story: Paul had spent about three years building the church in Ephesus (Acts 19; 20:31). When he said goodbye to its elders, he warned that false teachers would rise from among them (Acts 20:29-30). Now that has happened, and Paul, traveling on to Macedonia, has left his trusted coworker Timothy behind to deal with it. The chapter sets the terms for the whole letter. The problem is teaching that breeds speculation instead of faith and love. The answer is not only correct doctrine but the gospel of mercy, which Paul illustrates with his own story. Everything the letter goes on to say about worship, leaders, widows, and money rests on this foundation: a church shaped by the grace that saved the worst of sinners.
historical:
The letter is set after Paul has departed for Macedonia, the Roman province in northern Greece, leaving Timothy in Ephesus (verse 3). Those who hold that Paul wrote it usually place this after his first Roman imprisonment, around AD 62 to 64, in a period of travel that Acts does not record; those who see the Pastoral Letters as the work of a later follower date it later, often between about AD 80 and 110 (see the introduction). Either way, the situation is that of a church a generation or less old, facing teachers from within its own ranks.

What exactly the false teachers taught is not fully clear, because Paul describes it only in passing. Here they are said to be fascinated with myths and endless genealogies and to want to be teachers of the law (verses 4 and 7). Later chapters add that they forbade marriage and certain foods (4:3), treated religion as a source of profit (6:5), and claimed special knowledge (6:20). Many scholars see a mix of Jewish speculation, perhaps elaborate stories built on the family lists and figures of the Old Testament, with ascetic practice. Some have seen an early form of the movements later called Gnostic, which prized secret knowledge; others think that label comes too early and that the teaching fits the first century well enough on its own.
cultural:
Two of the men involved are named: Hymenaeus and Alexander (verse 20). Hymenaeus appears again in 2 Timothy 2:17-18 as teaching that the resurrection had already happened. An Alexander the coppersmith who did Paul great harm appears in 2 Timothy 4:14, though whether he is the same man is uncertain, since the name was common. To hand someone over to Satan (compare 1 Corinthians 5:5) most likely means removing him from the fellowship of the church, putting him back outside the community where Satan's power is at work, with the aim of correction: they are handed over “to be taught not to blaspheme.”

The list of lawbreakers in verses 9-10 follows the order of the second half of the Ten Commandments, which a Jewish or Jewish-Christian reader would have recognized: dishonoring parents (killers of father or mother), murder, adultery (the sexually immoral and those who practice homosexual acts), stealing (slave traders, who in the ancient world often kidnapped people for sale), and false witness (liars and perjurers). The word the BSB translates “homosexuals” (arsenokoitai) is rare. It appears to be formed from the Greek words used in the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament) at Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, and most scholars and the church's historic teaching read it as referring to men who engage in sexual relations with men. A minority of interpreters argue that it refers more narrowly to exploitative practices such as those involving slaves or boys. Paul's point in the list is that the law exposes sin; the list ends by setting all these against sound teaching and the gospel.
literary: The chapter opens with the standard ancient letter greeting, enriched in a Christian way with grace, mercy, and peace (verse 2). It then moves in three steps. Verses 3-11 state the problem and set the law in its place. Verses 12-17 turn from the false teachers to Paul's own story of mercy, and at its center stands the first of five “trustworthy sayings” in the Pastoral Letters (verse 15), probably a well-known summary of the faith that Paul quotes and affirms. That section closes in a burst of praise (verse 17), a doxology or formal word of glory to God. Verses 18-20 return to Timothy with a charge framed in military language (the good fight, or warfare) and a nautical image of shipwreck. The contrast running through the chapter is between speculation that goes nowhere and the plain gospel that saves.

outline.t: Greeting to Timothy, a true child in the faith
Stop the false teachers: the goal is love
The right use of the law
Mercy to the worst of sinners, and praise to the eternal King
Fight the good fight: faith, conscience, and shipwreck

doctrines.note: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (verse 15) is one of the plainest statements of the gospel in the New Testament. Paul's own conversion shows that no one is beyond God's mercy, and that grace is given, not earned.

The law “is good, if one uses it legitimately” (verse 8). Its role here is to restrain and expose sin, not to serve as material for speculation or as a ladder to righteousness. Paul affirms the law and refuses its misuse.
The doxology of verse 17 calls God the King eternal, immortal, invisible, and the only God. The false teachers' myths shrink God into a puzzle; Paul answers with worship.

words.note: Hugiainō, to be healthy or sound. From it comes the Pastoral Letters' phrase “sound teaching” (verse 10), literally healthy teaching. The image is medical: true teaching produces spiritual health, while false teaching spreads like disease. The word appears often in these letters and rarely elsewhere in Paul.

Oikonomia, the management of a household, stewardship. In verse 4 it describes God's ordering of his work of salvation, which people enter by faith, set against speculation that produces only questions. It anticipates the letter's picture of the church as God's household (3:15).

Eleeō, to show mercy. Paul says twice that he “was shown mercy” (verses 13 and 16). The passive voice matters: Paul did nothing to secure it. His story becomes a display case of Christ's patience for everyone who would later believe.

Suneidēsis, conscience, the inner awareness that judges one's own conduct. It appears in verses 5 and 19 and becomes a key word in the Pastoral Letters. A good conscience is the ship's hull; reject it and faith runs aground.

christ: The chapter's center is a sentence about Jesus: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (verse 15). The phrase “came into the world” assumes that he existed before his human birth, echoing the way John's Gospel speaks of him (John 1:9-11). Paul does not present Christ as a teacher of better religious ideas, which is what the false teachers were selling, but as a rescuer of the undeserving. In Paul himself, a violent persecutor of the church, Christ put his “perfect patience” on display as a pattern for all who would believe (verse 16). The chapter also speaks of Christ Jesus as the one who strengthened Paul and appointed him to service, the Lord who equips those he calls. Paul's story is meant to reassure every later reader that the mercy that reached him can reach them.

hard.q: What does it mean that Paul handed two men “over to Satan”?
hard.a:
The phrase sounds harsh, and it is meant to be serious. Most interpreters understand it as a form of church discipline: formally removing a person from the fellowship of the church and so placing him back in the world outside, which the New Testament sees as the sphere where Satan's power operates. Paul uses similar language in 1 Corinthians 5:5, where the aim is that the person's spirit may be saved. Some interpreters think it also involved physical suffering, as a kind of chastening, though the text does not say so.

What is clear is the purpose clause: they were handed over “to be taught not to blaspheme.” The discipline is meant to correct, not simply to punish or destroy. This fits the pattern elsewhere in Paul, where the one disciplined is still treated as a brother to be won back (2 Thessalonians 3:15). The difficulty for modern readers is less the idea of discipline than its severity, and here the context of teachers actively leading others away from the faith explains why Paul acted firmly.

questions: Paul says the goal of instruction is love from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith. How would that goal change the way you judge whether teaching is good?
Paul calls himself the worst of sinners, not the former worst. What does it do to a person to keep seeing himself or herself that way while being sure of mercy?
What are the modern equivalents of myths and endless genealogies, speculation that feels spiritual but produces only arguments?
